claim: Prdm9 is the only known vertebrate hybrid-sterility gene.
source: Prdm9, the only known vertebrate hybrid-sterility gene, causes failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and infertility in male hybrids that are the offspring of two mouse subspecies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about Prdm9.

claim: Prdm9 causes failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis in male hybrids that are offspring of two mouse subspecies.
source: Prdm9, the only known vertebrate hybrid-sterility gene, causes failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and infertility in male hybrids that are the offspring of two mouse subspecies.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Prdm9 causes infertility in male hybrids that are offspring of two mouse subspecies.
source: Prdm9, the only known vertebrate hybrid-sterility gene, causes failure of meiotic chromosome synapsis and infertility in male hybrids that are the offspring of two mouse subspecies.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Within species, Prdm9 determines the sites of programmed DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: Within species, Prdm9 determines the sites of programmed DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and meiotic recombination hotspots.
evidence: This is stated as an established function of Prdm9 within species.

claim: Within species, Prdm9 determines meiotic recombination hotspots.
source: Within species, Prdm9 determines the sites of programmed DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) and meiotic recombination hotspots.
evidence: This is stated as an established function of Prdm9 within species.

claim: Twenty-seven or more megabases of consubspecific homology fully restored synapsis in a given autosomal pair.
source: Twenty-seven or more megabases of consubspecific (belonging to the same subspecies) homology fully restored synapsis in a given autosomal pair, and we predicted that two or more DSBs within symmetric hotspots per chromosome are necessary for successful meiosis.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding reported in the abstract.

claim: Two or more DSBs within symmetric hotspots per chromosome are necessary for successful meiosis.
source: Twenty-seven or more megabases of consubspecific (belonging to the same subspecies) homology fully restored synapsis in a given autosomal pair, and we predicted that two or more DSBs within symmetric hotspots per chromosome are necessary for successful meiosis.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on the experimental data.

claim: Impaired recombination between evolutionarily diverged chromosomes could function as one of the mechanisms of hybrid sterility occurring in various sexually reproducing species.
source: We hypothesize that impaired recombination between evolutionarily diverged chromosomes could function as one of the mechanisms of hybrid sterility occurring in various sexually reproducing species.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a hypothesis in the abstract.

claim: Hybrid sterility is a postzygotic reproductive isolation mechanism that enforces speciation by restricting gene flow between related taxa.
source: Hybrid sterility (HS) is a postzygotic reproductive isolation mechanism that enforces speciation by restricting gene flow between related taxa.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Hybrid sterility is a universal phenomenon observed in many eukaryotic inter-species hybrids, including examples in yeast, plants, insects, birds, and mammals.
source: HS is a universal phenomenon observed in many eukaryotic inter-species hybrids, including examples in yeast, plants, insects, birds, and mammals (Coyne and Orr, 2004; Maheshwari and Barbash, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibility hypothesis explicates hybrid sterility as a consequence of the independent divergence of mutually interacting genes resulting in aberrant interaction of new alleles that have not been tested by natural selection.
source: In time, however, the Bateson–Dobzhansky–Muller incompatibility (BDMI) hypothesis (Muller and Pontecorvo, 1942; Dobzhansky, 1951; Orr, 1996) explicated HS, and more generally any hybrid incompatibility, as a consequence of the independent divergence of mutually interacting genes resulting in aberrant interaction of the new alleles that have not been tested by natural selection.
evidence: This is a description of an established hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Haldane's rule posits that if one sex of the F1 offspring of two different animal races is absent, rare, or sterile, it is the heterogametic sex (XY or ZW).
source: Haldane's rule posits that if one sex of the F1 offspring of two different animal races is absent, rare, or sterile, it is the heterogametic sex (XY or ZW) (Haldane, 1922).
evidence: This is a description of an established rule supported by citation.

claim: Chr X plays a disproportionately large role compared to autosomes in reproductive isolation.
source: Another common feature refers to the disproportionately large role of Chr X compared to that of autosomes in reproductive isolation (Presgraves, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a common feature supported by citation.

claim: Interaction between selfish genomic elements causing meiotic drive and their suppressors has been implicated in some instances of reproductive isolation.
source: More recently, interaction between selfish genomic elements causing meiotic drive and their suppressors has been implicated in some instances of reproductive isolation (Orr, 2005; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only five Drosophila HS genes have been identified to date: OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1.
source: In studies mapping HS genes, the Drosophila group of species has been the model of choice, yet only five Drosophila HS genes, namely OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1, have been identified to date, none of which has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis (Ting et al., 1998; Masly et al., 2006; Phadnis and Orr, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claim: None of the five identified Drosophila HS genes has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis.
source: In studies mapping HS genes, the Drosophila group of species has been the model of choice, yet only five Drosophila HS genes, namely OdsH, JYAlpha, Ovd, agt, and Taf1, have been identified to date, none of which has a known interacting partner predicted by the BDMI hypothesis (Ting et al., 1998; Masly et al., 2006; Phadnis and Orr, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claim: The first mouse HS locus Hst1 was genetically mapped in crosses of laboratory inbred strains with wild Mus musculus musculus mice.
source: The first mouse HS locus Hst1 was genetically mapped in crosses of laboratory inbred strains (predominantly of Mus musculus domesticus (Mmd) origin) with wild Mus musculus musculus (Mmm) mice (Forejt and Iványi, 1974).
evidence: This is a historical finding supported by citation.

claim: The Hst1 locus was identified with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9).
source: Finally, we identified the Hst1 locus with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9) (Mihola et al., 2009), which codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase (Powers et al., 2016) the first and still the only HS gene known in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a key finding supported by citation.

claim: Prdm9 codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase.
source: Finally, we identified the Hst1 locus with the PR-domain-containing nine gene (Prdm9) (Mihola et al., 2009), which codes for histone H3 lysine 4/lysine 36 methyltransferase (Powers et al., 2016) the first and still the only HS gene known in vertebrates.
evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citation.

claim: Most tested laboratory inbred strains share either the Prdm9Dom2 or the Prdm9Dom3 allele.
source: Most of the tested laboratory inbred strains share either the Prdm9Dom2 or the Prdm9Dom3 allele (Parvanov et al., 2010; Brunschwig et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a fact supported by citations.

claim: The male sterility of (PWD x C57BL/6)F1 hybrids depends on the interaction of the heterozygous allelic combination Prdm9Msc/Prdm9Dom2 with the PWD allelic form of the X-linked Hybrid sterility X Chromosome 2 locus, Hstx2Msc.
source: The male sterility of (PWD x C57BL/6)F1 (henceforth PB6F1) hybrids depends on the interaction of the heterozygous allelic combination Prdm9Msc/Prdm9Dom2 with the PWD allelic form of the X-linked Hybrid sterility X Chromosome 2 locus, Hstx2Msc (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a key finding supported by citations.

claim: Less than 10% instead of the expected 25% of (PWD x B6) x B6 male backcross progeny replicated the infertility of male PB6F1 hybrids.
source: The proper allelic combination of Prdm9 and Hstx2 genes is necessary but not sufficient to govern HS completely because less than 10% instead of the expected 25% of (PWD x B6) x B6 male backcross progeny replicated the infertility of male PB6F1 hybrids (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by citation.

claim: Approximately 90% of primary spermatocytes of infertile PB6F1 hybrids have multiple unsynapsed autosomal pairs decorated by phosphorylated histone γH2AX as a mark of persisting unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks.
source: We observed multiple unsynapsed autosomal pairs decorated by phosphorylated histone γH2AX as a mark of persisting unrepaired DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in approximately 90% of primary spermatocytes of infertile PB6F1 hybrids.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The asynapsis in PB6F1 hybrids was accompanied by disturbed transcriptional inactivation of sex chromosomes at the first meiotic prophase.
source: The asynapsis was accompanied by disturbed transcriptional inactivation of sex chromosomes at the first meiotic prophase (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is an observation supported by citations.

claim: Replacement of the mouse sequence encoding the PRDM9 zinc-finger array with the orthologous human sequence reversed sterility in (PWD x B6-Prdm9Hu)F1 hybrid males.
source: Recently, the role of PRDM9 zinc-finger-domain binding sites within noncoding genomic DNA has been demonstrated in PB6F1 male HS. Replacement of the mouse sequence encoding the PRDM9 zinc-finger array with the orthologous human sequence reversed sterility in (PWD x B6-Prdm9Hu)F1 hybrid males (Davies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: In PB6F1 hybrids, roughly 70% of the Prdm9-directed DSBs hotspots identified by the DMC1 ChIP-seq method were enriched on the 'nonself' homologous chromosome.
source: In PB6F1 hybrids, roughly 70% of the Prdm9-directed DSBs hotspots identified by the DMC1 ChIP-seq method were enriched on the 'nonself' homologous chromosome, as the DSB hotspots determined by the B6 allele of Prdm9 were found predominantly on PWD chromosomes, and vice versa.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on ChIP-seq data.

claim: Chromosome-specific quantification of asymmetry correlated well with the asynapsis rate across five arbitrarily chosen chromosomes of PB6F1 hybrids.
source: Chromosome-specific quantification of asymmetry correlated well with the asynapsis rate across five arbitrarily chosen chromosomes of PB6F1 hybrids (Davies et al., 2016; Smagulova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: One third of PRDM9-dependent DSBs were reported within sequences that have at least some repetitive character.
source: Recently, one third of PRDM9-dependent DSBs were reported within sequences that have at least some repetitive character, indicating that inappropriately high DSB levels in transposons and other repetitive elements may contribute to the infertility seen in some mouse hybrids (Yamada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: All autosomes of PB6F1 hybrid males displayed a certain degree of asynapsis, with frequencies ranging from 2.6% (Chr 1) to 42.2% (Chr 19).
source: All autosomes of hybrid males displayed a certain degree of asynapsis, classified as complete, partial, or intermingled (more than two tangled univalents within labeled chromatin cloud), with frequencies ranging from 2.6% (Chr 1) to 42.2% (Chr 19) (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: The five smallest autosomes had higher asynapsis rates (p=5.2×10−14).
source: A strong bias was evident towards higher asynapsis rates in the five smallest autosomes (p=5.2×10−14, comparison of Generalized Linear Mixed Models [GLMM], Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation (Spearman's ρ=−0.760, p=0.0003) between asynapsis rate and predicted symmetric DSBs.
source: Under these conditions, a strong negative correlation (Spearman's ρ=−0.760, p=0.0003) of asynapsis rate with predicted symmetric DSBs (Lange et al., 2016) can be seen (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The correlation between asynapsis rate and symmetric DSB hotspots is stronger than the correlation between asynapsis rate and chromosomal physical length.
source: This correlation is stronger than the correlation of the asynapsis rate with the chromosomal physical length (Spearman's ρ=−0.681, p=0.0013).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from the study.

claim: Symmetric DSBs add an additional explanation of the asynapsis rate to that provided by the chromosomal length (p=0.046).
source: On the contrary, the symmetric DSBs add an additional explanation of the asynapsis rate to that provided by the chromosomal length (p=0.046, comparison of GLMM models).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: Synapsis of a pair of homologous chromosomes depends on the presence of a certain minimum number of symmetric DSBs.
source: Thus, our findings suggest that synapsis of a pair of homologous chromosomes depends on the presence of a certain minimum number of symmetric DSBs, as we elaborate further using a simulation described in the 'Discussion'.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data and modeling.

claim: Subnuclear regions of asynapsed chromosomes composed of sex chromosomes and/or autosomal univalents were lacking active euchromatin in contrast to other regions of the pachytene nuclei.
source: Fluorescence signal quantification revealed that subnuclear regions of asynapsed chromosomes composed of sex chromosomes and/or autosomal univalents were lacking active euchromatin in contrast to other regions of the pachytene nuclei (Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from fluorescence microscopy.

claim: The absence of active euchromatin is a consequence of the meiotic synapsis failure of intersubspecific chromosomes, known as meiotic silencing of unsynapsed chromatin (MSUC).
source: We propose that the absence of active euchromatin is a consequence of the meiotic synapsis failure of intersubspecific chromosomes, known as meiotic silencing of unsynapsed chromatin (MSUC [Burgoyne et al., 2009]), which can act as an epigenetic component contributing to the meiotic phenotypes of sterile hybrids (Larson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Meiotic asynapsis affects intersubspecific (PWD/B6) but not consubspecific (PWD/PWD) pairs of homologous chromosomes in sterile male hybrids.
source: We have shown previously that meiotic asynapsis affects intersubspecific (PWD/B6) but not consubspecific (PWD/PWD) pairs of homologous chromosomes in sterile male hybrids from crosses of PWD females and B6.PWD-Chr # consomic males (Gregorová et al., 2008; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a previous finding supported by citations.

claim: All male progeny of the 2-chr crosses were fully sterile, with low testis weight and the absence of sperm in the epididymis.
source: All male progeny of the 2-chr crosses were fully sterile, with low testis weight and the absence of sperm in the epididymis.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Introduction by recombination of 27 Mb or more of a consubspecific (PWD/PWD) interval into a pair of intersubspecific (PWD/B6) homologs effectively suppressed the asynapsis rate below the baseline of 5% in all six studied autosomes.
source: Introduction by recombination of 27 Mb or more of a consubspecific (PWD/PWD) interval into a pair of intersubspecific (PWD/B6) homologs effectively suppressed the asynapsis rate below the baseline of 5% in all six studied autosomes (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding from the study.

claim: The change point for synapsis rescue was estimated at 27.14 Mb (19.36; 34.91) (95% CI).
source: The model based on the data pooled from all 2-chr crosses was selected as the best model with an estimated change point at 27.14 Mb (19.36; 34.91) (95% CI) (see Figure 3—source data 7).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: The location of the consubspecific sequence at the telomeric end was not essential for synapsis (p=0.9573).
source: In spite of the known role of subtelomeric (bouquet) association in chromosome pairing (Ishiguro et al., 2014; Scherthan et al., 2014), the location of the consubspecific sequence at the telomeric end was not essential for synapsis (p=0.9573, F-test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: PWD/PWD intervals of sufficient size rescued synapsis whether located at the centromeric (proximal, n = 14 cases), interstitial (n = 3), or telomeric (distal, n = 14) position.
source: The PWD/PWD intervals of sufficient size rescued synapsis whether located at the centromeric (proximal, n = 14 cases), interstitial (n = 3), or telomeric (distal, n = 14) position (Figure 3—source data 1–6).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: Complete elimination of asynapsis of four of the shortest autosomes could increase the proportion of primary spermatocytes that have the full set of synapsed autosomes up to 26.7%.
source: Provided that hybrid male sterility is directly dependent on chromosome synapsis, we predicted (by multiplying the probabilities of the synapsis of individual chromosomes obtained in F1 hybrids) that complete elimination of asynapsis of four of the shortest autosomes (excluding Chr 17 to avoid Prdm9PWD/PWD interference) could increase the proportion of primary spermatocytes that have the full set of synapsed autosomes up to 26.7% and could potentially abolish the apoptosis of these cells to yield around 5 million sperm cells in the epididymis of the hybrid males.
evidence: This is a prediction based on calculations from the data.

claim: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic.
source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: In the 4-chr cross, 19.5% of males had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count.
source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: In the 4-chr cross, 28.7% of males had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells.
source: In the PB6F1 cross, 100% of hybrid males displayed no sperm in the epididymis, whereas in the 4-chr cross, only 51.7% of 87 G4 males were aspermic, 19.5% had a 0.01–0.74 × 106 sperm count, and 28.7% had 1.0–13.7 × 106 sperm cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the study.

claim: The hybrids had sperm when asynapsis was suppressed in at least three of four segregating chromosomes and when the probability of all four consomic chromosomes being synapsed was >0.7 (p=0.0014).
source: As a rule of thumb, the hybrids had sperm when asynapsis was suppressed in at least three of four segregating chromosomes and when the probability of all four consomic chromosomes being synapsed was >0.7 (p=0.0014, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: In PB6F1 hybrids, the observed 13.1% (11.4–14.9%) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas was double (p=0.023) the 6.6% (5.3–8.1%) rate expected by the multiplication of the observed synapsis rates of individual chromosomes.
source: First, in PB6F1 hybrids, the observed 13.1% (11.4–14.9%) (95% CI) of fully synapsed pachynemas was double (p=0.023, Mann-Whitney test) the 6.6% (5.3–8.1%) rate expected by the multiplication of the observed synapsis rates of individual chromosomes (Figure 5—source data 1), indicating a trans effect of synapsed autosomes on the probability of the asynapsis of other PWD/B6 chromosome pairs.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study indicating a trans effect.

claim: The asynapsis rate of nonrecombinant PWD/B6 chromosomes was dramatically reduced in 2-chr crosses or the 4-chr cross (odds ratio [OR]=0.687, p=0.0002) compared to F1 hybrid rates.
source: Second, at the level of individual chromosomes, the most straightforward comparison was between the nonrecombinant PWD/B6 chromosomes, where the asynapsis rate was dramatically reduced in 2-chr crosses or the 4-chr cross (odds ratio [OR]=0.687, p=0.0002, GLMM) compared to F1 hybrid rates.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: If the predicted synapsis rate of three chromosomes is increased by ten percent, we can expect a 4.18% (2.72–5.34%) (95% CI) decrease of asynapsis rate of the fourth chromosome (p=0.0266).
source: On average, if the predicted synapsis rate of three chromosomes is increased by ten percent, we can expect a 4.18% 2.72–5.34%) (95% CI) decrease of asynapsis rate of the fourth chromosome (p=0.0266, log-log regression).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: For chromosomes with at least 34.9 Mb of PWD/PWD segment, the trans effect could not be detected (p=0.186).
source: However, for the chromosomes with at least 34.9 Mb of PWD/PWD segment (right bound of 95% CI of change point estimate), for which an additional length of PWD/PWD was not shown to affect asynapsis rate anymore, the trans effect could not be detected (p=0.186, comparison of GLMM models).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the study.

claim: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes.
source: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes and by partial recovery in Prdm9PWD/C3H males (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Davies et al., 2016), but a chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: The chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
source: The genic control of HS and meiotic synapsis in PB6F1 hybrids can be demonstrated by complete restitution of fertility and meiotic pairing in males with Prdm9PWD/PWD or Prdm9PWD/B6Hu genotypes and by partial recovery in Prdm9PWD/C3H males (Dzur-Gejdosova et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Davies et al., 2016), but a chromosome-autonomous nature of asynapsis became apparent in experiments where PB6F1 hybrids carried a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The males with a single pair of PWD/PWD consubspecific homologs remained sterile, but the synapsis of the particular consubspecific pair was completely restored.
source: The males remained sterile, but the synapsis of the particular consubspecific pair was completely restored (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citation.

claim: The DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of the PRDM9 molecule is responsible for sterility in PB6F1 hybrids.
source: Davies et al. (2016) found that the DNA-binding zinc-finger domain of the PRDM9 molecule is responsible for sterility in PB6F1 hybrids.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Most PRDM9PWD-specific hotspots reside on B6 chromosomes and most of the PRDM9B6-binding sites are activated on PWD chromosomes.
source: Further, they found that in the sterile hybrids, most PRDM9PWD-specific hotspots reside on B6 chromosomes and, vice versa, that most of the PRDM9B6-binding sites are activated on PWD chromosomes.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: The asymmetry of PRDM9 hotspots could be explained in part by erosion of the PRDM9-binding sites due to preferential transmission to progeny of the altered hotspots motifs.
source: This asymmetry could be explained in part by erosion of the PRDM9-binding sites due to preferential transmission to progeny of the altered hotspots motifs (Boulton et al., 1997; Myers et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an explanation supported by citations.

claim: A similar pattern of higher sensitivity of smaller autosomes to the synapsis failure was observed in mice with lowered dosages of SPO11.
source: A similar pattern of higher sensitivity of smaller autosomes to the synapsis failure was observed in mice with lowered dosages of SPO11 (Kauppi et al., 2013) and in the consequent two-fold DSB reduction.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Synaptonemal complexes nucleate at multiple recombination sites in each chromosome.
source: We found that chromosomes with 27 Mb or longer stretches of consubspecific sequence always rescued full synapsis in hybrid males. The position of the consubspecific interval along the chromosome was not critical for synapsis rescue, in accordance with the finding that synaptonemal complexes nucleate at multiple recombination sites in each chromosome (Zickler and Kleckner, 2015; Finsterbusch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Two symmetric DSBs per chromosome could be sufficient for full development of the synaptonemal complex.
source: Thus, it is consistent with our data that two symmetric DSBs per chromosome could be sufficient for full development of the synaptonemal complex, as shown in Figure 6 (slope of the regression of P[asynapsis] on P[0 or one symmetric DSBs]=1.00).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on modeling and data analysis.

claim: In approximately 25% of cases, a chromosome is asynapsed because there are only asymmetric DSBs and no symmetric DSBs.
source: Our model predicts that in approximately 25% of cases, a chromosome is asynapsed because there are only asymmetric DSBs and no symmetric DSBs (slope of the regression of P[asynapsis] on P[0 symmetric DSBs]=4.22).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: The trans effect refers to the enhanced probability of synapsis of a pair of intersubspecific homologs depending on successful pairing of other chromosomes in males with the Prdm9PWD/Prdm9B6, Hstx2PWD 'hybrid sterility' genotype.
source: The trans effect as reported in this paper refers to the enhanced probability of synapsis of a pair of intersubspecific homologs depending on successful pairing of other chromosomes in males with the Prdm9PWD/Prdm9B6, Hstx2PWD 'hybrid sterility' genotype.
evidence: This is a definition of the trans effect observed in the study.

claim: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule.
source: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule (Haldane, 1922) but their oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
evidence: This is an observation supported by citation.

claim: PB6F1 hybrid female oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
source: PB6F1 hybrid females are fertile, obeying Haldane's rule (Haldane, 1922) but their oogenesis is impaired, having 45% of pachynemas with one or more asynapsed autosomes.
evidence: This is an experimental observation.

claim: The effect of Prdm9 on asynapsis in female PB6F1 meiosis seems weak or absent.
source: Nevertheless, the effect of Prdm9 on asynapsis in female PB6F1 meiosis seems weak or absent (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: Ninety percent of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs.
source: However, quantitative meiotic analyses revealed that 90% of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs and, more importantly, that asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: Asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions.
source: However, quantitative meiotic analyses revealed that 90% of primary spermatocytes carry one or more pairs of asynapsed homologs and, more importantly, that asynapsis is chromosome-autonomous, depending on inter-homolog (cis-) interactions (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013, 2014).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: By deliberately manipulating the synapsis of homologous chromosomes, we could modify the extent of meiotic arrest in intersubspecific PB6F1 hybrids in a predictable way.
source: The findings described in this paper provide the first direct link between Prdm9-controlled asynapsis and meiotic arrest in PB6F1 male hybrids. We showed that by deliberately manipulating the synapsis of homologous chromosomes, we could modify the extent of meiotic arrest in intersubspecific PB6F1 hybrids in a predictable way.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the study.

claim: A particular chromosome fails to synapse in as few as 2% and maximally in 45% of PB6F1 pachynemas.
source: A particular chromosome fails to synapse in as few as 2% and maximally in 45% of PB6F1 pachynemas.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The B6 allele of the X-linked Hstx2 locus dramatically increases the pairing efficiency but causes only a small change, if any alteration, in the profile of asymmetric hotspots.
source: Oddly, the B6 allele of the X-linked Hstx2 locus dramatically increases the pairing efficiency but causes only a small change, if any alteration, in the profile of asymmetric hotspots (Davies et al., 2016; Smagulova et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding supported by citations.

claim: The mechanisms that safeguard recombination between homologous allelic sequences could function as checkpoints that disable recombination after homologous sequences have diverged sufficiently during the isolation of closely related taxa.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the mechanisms that safeguard recombination between homologous allelic sequences could function as checkpoints that disable recombination after homologous sequences have diverged sufficiently during the isolation of closely related taxa.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The role of the mismatch repair system in reproductive isolation has been reported in Saccharomyces species.
